4.6.2 
Design 
Any failure from which potentially hazardous conditions are a risk shall cause the system to revert to 
conditions that will be safest for personnel and with the lowest property damage potential. 
4.6.3 
Redundant Features 
This Guide recommends that redundant safety features (such as relief valves, instrumentation, and 
controls) be installed when the failure of a single safety feature could cause a mishap, which might result 
in loss of mission, property, or personnel. 
 
Safety Assessment and Mishap Reporting 
4.7.1 
Safety Review 
All plans, designs, and operations associated with hydrogen use must be subject to an independent safety 
review by a group of knowledgeable experts not directly connected with the activity.  Safety reviews should 
include effects of fluid properties, training, escape and rescue, fire detection, and fire fighting.  A safety 
review is required by 29 CFR 1910.119. 
4.7.2 
Operating Procedures 
Operating procedures for normal and emergency conditions shall be established and reviewed as 
appropriate.  Written operating procedures are required by 29 CFR 1910.103 and 29 CFR 1910.119. 
4.7.3 
Hazard Analyses 
Hazard analyses should be performed to identify conditions that may cause injury, death, mission delay or 
loss, or property damage. For quantities of hydrogen greater than 4,536 kg (10,000 lb), a hazard analysis 
is required by 29 CFR 1910.119 and 29 CFR 1910.1200. 
4.7.4 
Mishap Reporting 
Reporting, investigating, and documenting the occurrences, causes, and corrective action required for 
mishaps, incidents, test failures, and mission failures shall follow established basic policy procedures and 
guidelines as specified by the AHJ.  For quantities of hydrogen greater than 4,536 kg (10,000 lb), mishap 
investigation and reporting are required by 29 CFR 1910.119. 
 
5 Properties and Hazards of Hydrogen 
Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, but, almost paradoxically, free hydrogen is rare in 
our environment; it is tied up in many chemical compounds and living organisms. It is not until hydrogen is 
isolated in bulk that concerns for safe handling arise. For the purpose of establishing safe practices, it is 
better to scrutinize equipment designs and operations for safety rather than consider hydrogen as a 
hazardous fluid.  
Sources of thermodynamic property information include ASTM D7265-12, Standard Specification for 
Hydrogen Thermophysical Property Property Tables, and National Institute of Standards and Technology, 
Standard Reference Database product REFPROP, version 9.0. 
 
Hydrogen Properties and Usage Hazards 
Hydrogen properties are introduced as they pertain to addressing safety concerns and understanding the 
creation of hazards. In order of the practical implications and the severity of consequences, concerns 
around hydrogen systems may be ranked from least to greatest as follows:

 
Consequences of personnel exposure and health after mitigation by design, operational controls, 
and personal protective equipment 
 
Hydrogen embrittlement of metals 
 
Low temperature exposure to system materials 
 
Inadvertent pressure release 
 
Inadvertent combustion including fire, deflagration, and detonation 
Aside from the utility derived from a hydrogen system, these are the issues that must be addressed for 
successful design and operation. 
5.1.1 
General Properties 
The physical properties of hydrogen derive from the low temperature phase behavior that governs the 
transition between solid, liquid, and gaseous states. Important parameters that convey this behavior are 
listed below: 
 
The triple point, the condition under which all three phases coexist (13.8 K and 7.2 kPa). 
NOTE.  This is a subatmospheric pressure.  
 
The critical temperature, or the highest temperature at which hydrogen vapor can be liquefied 
(approximately 33 K). 
 
The normal boiling point (NBP) at an absolute pressure of 1 atmosphere (101.323 kPa) is 20.3 K.  
This range of temperatures that defines the entire breadth of hydrogen phase behavior is very small.  
To the human senses, GH2 is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, and nontoxic gas. It is the lightest of all gases 
and, with approximately one-fifteenth the density of air, is very buoyant in ambient environments. Hydrogen 
can induce suffocation by diluting the concentration of oxygen below levels necessary to support life. 
Liquid hydrogen is colorless, odorless, noncorrosive, and not significantly reactive. LH2 has the lowest 
density of any liquefied gas. The boiling point temperature of LH2 at 1 atmosphere of pressure is below the 
freezing point of all other gases, with the exception of helium. These low temperatures present a severe 
frostbite hazard to human tissues if direct exposure occurs. When exposed to ambient heat, liquid hydrogen 
will expand in volume, vaporize, and expand as gas until at normal temperature and pressure (NTP) the 
total expansion over the original liquid volume with a factor of 845 times greater (McCarty, Hord, and Roder, 
1981). Safe handling of cryogenic hydrogen requires the use of pressure relief valves to avoid over-
pressurization, container rupture, and explosion hazards. 
Hydrogen, by itself, is chemically stable and in bulk will not undergo a chemical reaction when exposed to 
an ignition source. Of interest to aerospace applications is the ability for combustion of hydrogen with 
oxygen to produce a high specific impulse in rocket engines and as a fuel to power fuel cells. More recent 
electrolyzer and Sabatier applications use hydrogen in their process streams. Different applications require 
different storage systems, ranging from large dewars that contain liquid hydrogen to gas cylinders that 
supply standalone systems or laboratories. However, in any of these applications or operations that use 
hydrogen, inadvertent release of hydrogen can easily lead to combustion hazards because hydrogen is 
readily flammable with a variety of oxidizers. In air environments, hydrogen is flammable over a wide range 
of mixtures. Hydrogen and oxidizer mixtures can combust either as a fire at a fixed point or as a propagating 
flame in the form of a deflagration or detonation throughout a flammable mixture. 
The effect of hydrogen on materials typically used for containment is noncorrosive and considered 
nonreactive, but hydrogen will generally reduce the mechanical properties of some metals by a complex 
process commonly referred to as hydrogen embrittlement. When subject to rapid pressure cycling,

permeable materials, such as those found in seals, will suffer deterioration due to hydrogen gas expansion 
within the material. 
5.1.2 
Health Hazards 
Hydrogen gas is colorless, odorless, and not detectable in any concentration by human senses. Appropriate 
detection instrumentation  and control of hydrogen’s use are critical to safe operations.  
Although hydrogen is nontoxic and has no threshold limit value (TLV), it is classified as a simple asphyxiant 
and can result in asphyxiation by diluting the oxygen required in breathing air. An atmosphere containing 
oxygen at a concentration of less than 19.5% by volume is considered oxygen deficient. Note that hydrogen 
operations often use nitrogen and helium inert gases, which are asphyxiants, and they can present an 
equally great hazard to human health. 
Hydrogen is not listed as a carcinogen by the National Toxicology Program, International Agency Research 
on Cancer, or Occupational Safety and Health Administration.. 
Hydrogen burns with an almost invisible bluish flame. In daylight, the flame is so pale that the first indication 
of a hydrogen flame may be the feeling of heat or being burned rather than seeing the flame. The thermal 
radiation from a hydrogen flame is such that the flame may not be felt until direct contact with the flame's 
combustion products is made. 
Cryogenic burns are possible from contact with SLH2, LH2, cold GH2, or cold surfaces associated with their 
containment. Eyes can be injured by exposure to the cold gas or splashed liquid too brief to affect the skin 
of the hands or face. Contact between bare parts of the body with uninsulated piping or storage vessels 
containing SLH2, LH2, or cold GH2 can cause the flesh to stick and to tear when an attempt is made to break 
the contact. 
Exposure to blast, shrapnel, high-pressure burst, or jet of gas, either from a highly pressurized component 
or from combustion of hydrogen within a confined space, is possible upon catastrophic failure of a 
component containing hydrogen. 
Review Section 4.3.4 for specific health hazard data included in a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for GH2 and 
LH2.  See Annex E for more information on SDS content. 
 
Atomic and Molecular Properties 
In storage as a pure substance, hydrogen persists as a molecule with two hydrogen atoms sharing a 
covalent bond, and it is commonly designated H2. In the lattice structure of metal, hydrogen can exist in 
atomic form. 
5.2.1 
Atomic Properties 
Three isotopes of hydrogen are known: protium, with atomic mass 1; deuterium, with atomic mass 2 (one 
neutron); and tritium, with atomic mass 3 (two neutrons). Atomic hydrogen is created either by ionization or 
by dissociation of the covalent bond on a metal surface, freeing atomic hydrogen to permeate into a metal 
lattice. 
The focus of this Guide is on molecular hydrogen formed from protium. Deuterium exists only in trace 
quantities in nature, and tritium is a product of nuclear reactors. If deuterium and tritium are concentrated, 
then their physical properties will vary according to their greater atomic weights, and in sufficient quantities 
radioactivity may become a safety concern. The chemistry of all three isotopes is very nearly identical. 
At pressure exceeding 200 GPa to 300 GPa, SH2 can undergo transition into a metallic state and may be 
superconducting.

title: Molecular Properties and Characteristic Behaviors of Hydrogen
summary: This section details the molecular properties of hydrogen including ortho/parahydrogen forms and their thermal equilibrium behavior, thermophysical properties across various phases, and characteristic behaviors of gaseous hydrogen including dispersion, permeation, and thermal properties that distinguish it from other gases.
full_text:

21 
5.2.2 
Molecular Properties 
Each of the two atoms that make up a hydrogen molecule possesses a nuclear spin state, and together the 
total state of the molecule is characterized by the relative spins of the nuclei as being either parallel or 
antiparallel. The two forms (species) are designated orthohydrogen, for molecules with nuclear spins in the 
same direction (parallel), and parahydrogen, with nuclear spins in the opposite direction (antiparallel). 
Within a population of hydrogen molecules at thermal equilibrium, the relative number of each species that 
exists is governed by the temperature (see Figure 1). With a decrease in temperature, equilibrium favors 
the formation of parahydrogen. At a given temperature, once equilibrium is achieved, the mixture is referred 
to as equilibrium hydrogen. At ambient temperatures (in the vicinity of 300 K), the equilibrium mixture is 
designated normal hydrogen and possesses a content of 75% orthohydrogen and 25% parahydrogen. 
 
Figure 1 — Equilibrium percentage of parahydrogen vs. temperature (McCarty et al., 1981). 
 
During manufacture of liquid hydrogen, a cool-down process, also known as self-conversion, is 
accompanied by a release of heat. This release is significant, at approximately 500 J/g (220 Btu/lb) for the 
conversion of normal hydrogen at 300 K to parahydrogen at 20 K (see Annex C, Figure C1), and will cause 
significant liquid hydrogen boil-off losses, as much as 70%  of mass fraction. In addition, without the 
intervention of catalysts, the self-conversion proceeds slowly, taking over 1,000 hours for the bulk of the 
conversion to occur. Catalysts are used to accelerate this conversion in LH2 production facilities, which 
produce almost pure (95%) parahydrogen liquid. Commercially delivered LH2 has already undergone the 
conversion process to avoid excessive boil-off. 
There are some property differences in the different forms of hydrogen; thus, one must note the form for 
which the data are given. The orthohydrogen and parahydrogen molecules have slightly different physical 
properties but are chemically equivalent; therefore, the hazards associated with the use of hydrogen are 
the same irrespective of the molecular form.

5.2.3 
Hydrogen in a Metallic Lattice 
Hydrogen entry into a material may begin as permeation into small cracks and voids within a material. In 
the case of metals, a hydrogen molecule can adsorb onto the metal surface and then dissociate into atomic 
hydrogen. Hydrogen ions (H+) will readily diffuse by their very small size through a metal's crystal lattice. 
Within the metal, a variety of circumstances can arise, including 
 
Formation of a solid solution of hydrogen within the metal 
 
Formation of solid metal hydrides with alloy components within the metal 
 
Reformation into hydrogen molecules or other gaseous compounds within void spaces. 
These processes can result in increased crack growth within flaws and loss of strength within the bulk 
metal. Section 6.2 provides an overview of hydrogen embrittlement effects. 
 
Thermophysical Properties 
Selected thermophysical properties of various states of hydrogen, primarily parahydrogen, are given in the 
figures and tables in Annex C. McCarty, Hord, and Roder (1981) provide an extensive tabulation of the 
thermophysical properties of hydrogen: 
 
The vapor pressure of liquefied parahydrogen as a function of temperature from the triple point 
to the NBP is shown in Figure C2, and from the NBP to the critical point in Figure C3. 
 
Figure C4 gives the vapor pressure of parahydrogen and normal hydrogen below the triple 
point. 
 
Figure C5 gives a comparison of the densities and bulk fluid heat capacities for slush, triple-
point liquid, and NBP liquid parahydrogen. 
 
Figure C6 shows a proposed phase diagram (P-T plane) for SH2 at various ortho mole fractions. 
 
Figure C7 gives a proposed phase diagram (V-T plane) for solid normal hydrogen. 
 
Figure C8 shows the specific heat (heat capacity) of saturated SH2. 
 
Figure C9 gives the melting line from the triple point to the critical point pressure for 
parahydrogen. 
 
Selected thermophysical, chemical, and combustion properties of parahydrogen are provided 
in Table C1. This table presents property data for gaseous, liquid, slush, and solid phases. 
 
Table C2 gives some fixed-point properties of normal hydrogen. 
 
Table C3 gives a tabulation of thermodynamic properties of the hydrogen solid–vapor two-
phase region. 
 
Table C4 gives a tabulation of the thermodynamic properties of the hydrogen solid–liquid two-
phase region. 
 
Table C5 gives some data on the molar volume of compressed solid parahydrogen. 
 
Table C6 gives the thermal expansion coefficient of solid parahydrogen from 1 to 13.8 K 
(–458 °F to –435 °F). 
The thermodynamic properties of liquid and gaseous hydrogen in the ortho- and para- states can be 
calculated using computer programs such as Reference Fluid Thermodynamic and Transport Properties 
Database (REFPROP) available from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).  Online 
databases and calculation sources can be discovered using an Internet search engine.

Characteristic Behaviors of Hydrogen 
Knowledge of the general chemical and physical properties of hydrogen must be available to the designer 
and operators of hydrogen systems; some characteristics and properties are of particular concern for 
reasons of safety and hazard analyses and are discussed in the following subsections. 
5.4.1 
Gaseous Hydrogen  
GH2 disperses more readily than other gases when released in the open. Its density, buoyancy in air, and 
diffusivity must be considered for the case of inadvertent release, whether in the open or in and around 
structures where the possibility for full or partial confinement exists. When hydrogen is confined in tanks 
and lines, its ability to escape is greater than that of any other gases. Hydrogen's gaseous heat capacity, 
thermal conductivity, and Joule-Thomson (J-T) coefficient are also unique among gases. 
5.4.1.1 
Gaseous Dispersion 
Hydrogen possesses higher buoyancy and diffusivity than other gases. The density and specific gravity at 
the NTP of hydrogen is 0.0838 kg/m3 (5.2324 x 10-3 lb/ft3) and 0.0695 (air = 1), respectively. Therefore, 
hydrogen gas at ambient temperatures is approximately 14 times lighter than air, and when released in bulk 
at NTP, air will rise, with buoyant velocities ranging from 1.2 to 9 m/s (3.94 to 29.5 ft/s) (McCarty, Hord, and 
Roder, 1981). When confined in ducts and lines, hydrogen will seek a buoyant path out, and it has been 
observed to travel considerable distances and may create convection currents in so doing. In unventilated 
volumes, trapped hydrogen can accumulate. 
The diffusion coefficient for hydrogen in air (both at the NTP) is 0.61 cm2/s (0.095 in2/s) (McCarty, Hord, 
and Roder, 1981), which is greater than that of helium, approximately three times that of nitrogen, and four 
times that of natural gas under ambient conditions. 
The effects of wind can dominate the buoyancy and dispersion of hydrogen. 
5.4.1.2 
General Dispersion in Media 
Hydrogen in any concentration will always seek a path, where available, to greater dispersion. In addition 
to dispersion in gases, this includes penetration into confining walls of pressurized metal containers, 
entering into solution in fluids such as water, or permeation into materials. Hydrogen can disperse through 
multiple paths. For example, it can dissolve in water and then enter into vessel walls from the water. In 
general, hydrogen will tend to disperse such that concentration equilibrium is achieved within all adjacent 
spaces and media. Hydrogen may also be driven into media. Noteworthy circumstances of forced hydrogen 
dispersion occur in arc welding and electrochemical processes such as electroplating, electropolishing, and 
corrosion, all of which can introduce hydrogen into metals.  
5.4.1.3 
Viscosity 
Hydrogen's low viscosity (8.81 μPa · s at NTP) and small molecular size allow it to pass through porous 
materials, fittings, seals, and small cracks more readily than other fluids. The viscosity decreases as a 
function of temperature and is significantly less at cryogenic temperatures. 
5.4.1.4 
Gaseous Heat Capacity and Thermal Conductivity 
The gaseous heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and J-T coefficient distinguish hydrogen from other gases. 
The heat capacity at constant pressure (Cp) of hydrogen (30.02 J/mol · K [15.81 x 10-3 Btu/lbm °F] at NTP) 
is similar to that of other diatomic gases on a molar basis (consider air = 29.19 at 25 °C). However, on a 
weight basis, hydrogen's heat capacity at Cp (14.89 kJ/kg · K) is approximately 14 times larger than that of 
air. 
The thermal conductivity of hydrogen, 0.1914 mW/m · K (0.001327 Btu [IT] inch/hour/ft2/°F), is significantly 
greater than that of other gases (for example, more than seven times that of air).

Hydrogen permeation into metals occurs through surface adsorption, dissociation to atomic hydrogen, and diffusion through crystal lattice, potentially causing embrittlement
Gaseous hydrogen is approximately 14 times lighter than air with buoyant velocities of 1.2-9 m/s and diffusion coefficient of 0.61 cm²/s, enabling rapid dispersion
Hydrogen's low viscosity (8.81 μPa·s at NTP) and small molecular size allow penetration through porous materials, seals, and cracks more readily than other fluids
Hydrogen possesses exceptional heat capacity (14.89 kJ/kg·K, ~14 times that of air) and thermal conductivity (>7 times that of air)

title: Hydrogen Physical Properties and Hazard Characteristics (J-T Expansion, LH2, SLH2, SH2)
summary: Comprehensive technical overview of hydrogen behavior under various conditions including J-T expansion effects, liquefied hydrogen properties and hazards, slush hydrogen characteristics, and solid hydrogen phase information. Covers critical safety concerns such as cryogenic hazards, pressure generation, thermal effects, and contamination risks.
full_text:
--- Page 40 ---
ANSI/AIAA G-095A-2017 
 
24 
5.4.1.5 
J-T Expansion 
Most gases at ambient temperature are cooled by throttled expansion from high to low pressure. However, 
the temperature of hydrogen increases when it is expanded at a temperature and pressure outside the 
temperature and pressure conditions that define the J-T inversion curve for hydrogen. The maximum 
inversion temperature for hydrogen is 202 K (–96 °F) at an absolute pressure of zero (Walker, 1983); 
consequently, at any temperature and pressure condition greater than this, the temperature of hydrogen 
will increase upon expansion. 
The temperature increase as a result of a J-T expansion is not normally sufficient to be the source of ignition 
for a combustible hydrogen and oxidizer mixture. An example of the extent of the temperature rise is that 
the temperature of hydrogen initially at 300 K (80 °F) increases to 346 K (163 °F) when expanded from an 
absolute pressure of 100 MPa (14,500 psi) to an absolute pressure of 0.1 MPa (14.5 psi). A temperature 
rise of 46 K (83 °F) does not raise hydrogen to its ignition temperature unless it is already near the 
autoignition temperature of 858 K (1,085 °F). 
5.4.2 
Liquefied Hydrogen (LH2) 
All of the hazards that exist with GH2 also exist with LH2 because of the ease with which the liquid 
evaporates. Characteristic properties of LH2 also of particular concern for hazard analyses are discussed 
in the following subsections. 
5.4.2.1 
Boiling Point 
LH2 has an NBP of 20.3 K (–423.5 °F) at sea level. Any LH2 splashed on the skin or in the eyes can cause 
serious burns by frostbite or hypothermia. Inhaling vapor or cold gas produces respiratory discomfort, and 
asphyxiation can result. 
5.4.2.2 
Ice Formation 
Vents and valving from storage vessels and Dewars may be blocked by accumulations of ice formed from 
moisture in the air. Excessive pressure may then rupture the container and release hydrogen. 
5.4.2.3 
Liquid Air Formation 
Air in contact with uninsulated surfaces cooled by LH2 or cold hydrogen gas below about 82 K (–312 °F) 
can condense. This condensate will be enriched to about 50% oxygen. Any subsequent evaporation of the 
condensate can result in even further oxygen enrichment. Materials in the presence of an oxygen-enriched 
atmosphere can (depending on the material and various conditions) become combustible, and some can 
react explosively. 
5.4.2.4 
Solidification of Contaminants 
Storage vessels and other containers should be kept under positive pressure to prevent air from entering. 
LH2 is subject to contamination by condensed and solidified air from a variety of sources, such as improper 
purging. Oxygen can build up during repeated refilling or pressurization of permanent LH2 storage vessels. 
If the solid air is allowed to accumulate, vapors that form during warming of the vessel may form a flammable 
mixture within the vessel that is easily ignited. Nitrogen, often used as a purge gas, can also be condensed 
and solidified, and the solid particles of nitrogen can cause damage to components or cause failures such 
as preventing a valve from closing completely. 
5.4.2.5 
Continuous Evaporation 
The continuous evaporation of LH2 in a vessel generates GH2, which must be vented to a safe location or 
temporarily confined safely. This occurs in most Dewars or storage vessels as it is not feasible to sufficiently 
refrigerate liquid hydrogen. The gas generated by the evaporation of LH2 will eventually warm to the ambient 
temperature, giving a significant pressure rise if it is confined, as in a pipe between two valves. Considering 
GH2 as an ideal gas, the pressure resulting from a trapped volume of LH2 vaporizing and being heated to

294 K (70 °F) is 85.8 MPa (12,452 psia). However, the pressure is 172 MPa (25,000 psia) when hydrogen’s 
compressibility is considered. A significant pressure increase will occur in a system with only one phase 
present, and the LH2 experiences a temperature increase. A sample calculation for such a system is given 
in Annex F, Example 1. 
5.4.2.6 
Buoyancy of Cryogenic Vapors 
The cold, dense gases formed by releasing LH2 to the atmosphere contain saturated hydrogen vapor, which 
is heavier than air. Hydrogen at 23 K (–418.6 °F) is neutrally buoyant in ambient air. Buoyant velocities are 
related to the difference in air and hydrogen densities; therefore, the cold, dense hydrogen gases produced 
by LH2 spills will not rise until they warm. 
The cold, dense gases formed during a LH2 spill can collect in low terrain and remain close to the ground 
until the temperature rises. The higher density of saturated vapor vented from LH2 systems may cause a 
hydrogen cloud to flow horizontally or downward immediately upon release. Windblown or pressurized 
venting of saturated hydrogen vapors can travel along the ground for several hundred meters, depending 
upon conditions, before warming and rising. 
5.4.2.7 
Electric Charge Accumulation 
Measurements of the electrical conductivity of LH2 are found to have a typical resistivity of about 1019 ohm-
cm at 25 V and to be a linear function of applied voltage. It has been remarked that this indicates it is not 
strictly correct to consider the electrical conductivity of LH2 in terms of Ohm's Law (Willis, 1966). Although 
a current can be passed through LH2, this current can be explained in terms of charge carriers formed by 
background radiation. Thus, the current carrying capacity is small and more or less independent of the 
imposed voltage. Investigation has shown that electric charge buildup in flowing high-purity LH2 is not a 
great concern (Willis, 1966). 
5.4.3 
Slush Hydrogen  
SLH2 is a mixture of SH2 and LH2 at the triple point temperature. Properties of a 50% by mass solid or 50% 
by volume solid mixture usually are given, although other mass (or volume) fraction mixtures of solid and 
liquid are possible. 
All the hazards that exist with GH2 and LH2 also exist with SLH2. Additional system components are required 
to handle the two-phase SLH2; therefore, transfer and storage operations become more complex. 
Characteristic properties of SLH2 which are also of particular concern for hazard analyses are discussed in 
the following subsections. 
5.4.3.1 
Vapor Pressure 
The vapor pressure of SLH2 is 7.04 kPa (1 psia). Therefore, an SLH2 system is designed structurally to 
operate at pressures below atmospheric, and greater care must be taken during operations to prevent air 
leakage into the system. 
5.4.3.2 
Volume Change 
Heat leakage into SLH2 without ullage present requires the continual addition of high-solids-fraction SLH2 
and the removal of LH2 because SLH2 expands as it degrades. Significant increases in volume can occur 
when the solid phase of SLH2 melts (see Annex F, Example 1).  
5.4.3.3 
Thermal Stratification 
Thermal stratification of SLH2 storage can occur by design (a layer of LH2 on top of the SLH2, rising in 
temperature to 20.27 K [–423.5 °F] and an equilibrium pressure of 101.3 kPa [14.7 psia]), or by operation 
(such as introducing helium [He] into the ullage space for pressure control). Upsetting the thermal 
stratification can lead to hazardous pressure changes in both cases (Edeskuty and Stewart, 1996).

5.4.3.4 
Thermal Acoustic Oscillation 
Thermal acoustic oscillation (TAO) can occur whenever a long tube connects a region at cryogenic 
temperature with an ambient-temperature region (300 K, 80 F°). Instrumentation lines and ports for fluid 
flow are examples where these conditions can exist. TAO is of concern for liquid hydrogen because of the 
low temperature and other pertinent thermophysical properties. TAO can occur without any net flow of fluid 
or any intended transfer of heat (Edeskuty and Stewart, 1996). TAO can lead to pressure surges in LH2 
and SLH2 systems. Egress of LH2 or SLH2 into warmer instrument or discharge lines causes vaporization 
and a pressure increase, which forces the LH2 or SLH2 gas back to the bulk LH2 or SLH2, where cooling 
causes a reverse surge. Such oscillations result in an increased heat input to the bulk LH2 or SLH2. 
5.4.3.5 
Aging 
Aging of SH2 particles in SLH2 can result in particle settling or change in critical flow velocity of the SLH2. 
Subsequent settling would result in over-pressurization of the SLH2 flow (Edeskuty and Stewart, 1996). 
5.4.3.6 
Electric Charge Buildup 
Although investigation has shown that electric charge buildup in flowing LH2 is not a great concern, the 
potential accumulation of electric charge in flowing SLH2 has not been definitively excluded. The elimination 
of ignition sources may be compromised during SLH2 flow operations (Edeskuty and Stewart, 1996). 
5.4.3.7 
Ortho- to Parahydrogen Conversion 
At one stage during the liquefaction process of LH2, the product stream is at least 95% parahydrogen. The 
heat generation by this residual ortho- to parahydrogen conversion acts as an additional heat leak into the 
system. This conversion is slow but finite if no catalyst is present. At 20 K (–424 °F), the heat of conversion 
for normal hydrogen is 527 J/g (226 Btu/lb). Annex F, Example 2, contains an analysis of heat leak and 
ortho- to parahydrogen conversion in an SLH2 system. Equilibrium at the SLH2 temperature 13.8 K (–435.2 
°F) has shifted to 100% parahydrogen; therefore, any orthohydrogen will have been converted to 
parahydrogen. 
5.4.3.8 
Helium Solubility 
The solubility of helium in SLH2 is a concern if helium is used to pressurize the SLH2 storage vessel. 
Potential safety issues include altering the helium pressurization gas requirements (and hence pressure 
control), influencing the temperature gradient within the vapor phase of the storage vessel (affecting helium 
pressurization gas requirements), and changing the pumping characteristics of the SLH2. Although it has 
not been determined for SLH2, several reports are available for the solubility of helium in LH2 over a range 
of temperature and pressure (Smith, 1952; Streett, Sonntag, and Van Wylen, 1964). 
5.4.4 
Solid Hydrogen (SH2) 
At temperatures well below 14 K, hydrogen assumes face centered cubic (FCC) and hexagonal close 
packed (HPC) crystalline forms. Within the SH2 P-T plane, the morphology is made complex by the atomic 
structure of one proton and one electron and by the orthohydrogen and parahydrogen molecular spin. FCC 
structures exist below approximately 3 K, but they also exist at pressures between 50 and 500 atmospheres. 
Because liquid hydrogen possesses few contaminants, formation of solid states typically occurs well below 
the triple point due to supercooling effects. 
From a safety perspective, the issues associated with SH2 parallel that of SLH2. SH2 possesses greater 
density than liquid hydrogen, and at the triple point a phase change from solid to liquid is accompanied by 
a greater than 11% volume growth. More detailed information may be found in the literature (McCarty, Hord, 
and Roder, 1981).

title: Combustion-Related Properties of Hydrogen
summary: This section from ANSI/AIAA G-095A-2017 describes the combustion characteristics of hydrogen, including flame temperature profiles, flame color properties, and emission spectra. Hydrogen combustion requires mixing with an oxidizer within reaction limits and an ignition source, with behavior influenced by pressure, temperature, gravity, and confinement geometry. Key safety considerations include the colorless nature of hydrogen flames and extreme flame temperatures reaching up to 3,824°F in stoichiometric air mixtures.

27 
 
Combustion-Related Properties 
The flammability, ignition, and combustion properties and behaviors of hydrogen are considered the most 
important factors in understanding the hazards associated with a hydrogen system. 
5.5.1 
General 
Combustion reactions require that hydrogen be mixed with an oxidizer, that the mixture be within reaction 
limits, and that a sufficiently energetic ignition source be present to initiate combustion. Combustion is 
influenced by the relative amounts of hydrogen and oxidizer; the presence of diluents; and the physical 
conditions of flow, pressure, temperature, and gravity. Also playing a role in the behavior of combustion are 
the circumstances of how hydrogen mixes with the oxidizer when ignition occurs, such as a small leak into 
air, a high-pressure turbulent jet, cryogenic liquid flashing into air, or the reactants being premixed over a 
volume. The presence of confining surfaces and their geometry can influence combustion behavior in 
dramatic ways, typically by absorbing ignition energies, or by coupling expansion of hot product gases with 
fluid flow. Mixtures with a near-stoichiometic composition are very sensitive to ignition, even from extremely 
weak ignition sources, and for practical purposes can be said to ignite spontaneously. Several modes of 
combustion depend on how reactive species are brought together and mixed: by simple diffusion of reactive 
species (laminar burning), by diffusion enhanced by flow (deflagration), and by shockwaves (detonation). 
Most combustion scenarios involve mixing reactants in gaseous form, but extremely energetic mixtures are 
possible if species mix as cryogenic liquids and/or solids. Each mode possesses unique reaction limits. 
Sections 5.5.2 through 5.5.6 address reactions that occur in gaseous mixtures, whereas Section 5.5.7 
addresses the less common condensed phase reactions. 
5.5.2 
Combustion Characteristics 
For safety reasons, personnel working in the vicinity of hydrogen sources must understand several very 
important physical characteristics of hydrogen combustion. 
5.5.2.1 
Lack of Flame Color 
Hydrogen-air and hydrogen-oxygen flames are colorless, and any visibility is caused by impurities. At 
reduced pressures, a pale blue or purple flame may be present. Severe burns have been inflicted on 
persons exposed to hydrogen flames that result from the ignition of hydrogen gas escaping from leaks and 
ruptures. 
5.5.2.2 
Flame Temperature in Air 
The flame temperature varies with the mixture content of the combustion reaction. In air, at 1 atmosphere, 
and beginning at 298 K (76.7 °F), the temperature of combustion products ranges from less than 800 K 
(980 °F) at the lower flammability limit (LFL) to 2,380 K (3,824 °F) for a stoichiometric mixture (29.5% H2 
v/v) (Rivkin, 2005), and to approximately 1,300 K (1,880 °F) at the upper flammability limit (UFL). Table 1 
gives the calculated characteristics of several mixtures of hydrogen-air-oxygen based on chemical 
equilibrium calculations (Gordon and McBride, 1994).

5.5.2.4 
Emissivity 
The capability of flames to heat the environment and present a thermal radiation hazard can be 
characterized by their apparent or average emissivity. Flame emissivity is the ratio of the energy radiated 
per unit area of the flame envelope to the energy per unit area radiated by a blackbody surface at the same 
temperature. The emissivity of hydrogen is reported to vary from 0.01 to 0.10 depending on various factors, 
including time delay before ignition, the assumed flame temperature, the quantity of liquid spilled, or amount 
of gas released, and atmospheric absorption. The water vapor forming within large combusting clouds of 
hydrogen that possess dimensions approaching 10 m or greater will absorb and reradiate over a broad 
range of frequencies and approach the emission spectra characteristic of a blackbody radiator (Weiser, 
2007). 
These values for hydrogen are notable because our practical experience with exposure to flames derives 
from hydrocarbon flames that have an emissivity approaching 1.0. Therefore, in comparison to hydrocarbon 
flames of equivalent size, direct exposure of surfaces in proximity to hydrogen flames will see 1% to 10%  as 
much radiation. This poses a safety concern to personnel, who in addition to not being able to see a 
hydrogen flame in ambient light, may not be able to adequately sense heat in proximity to a hydrogen flame 
(Chelton, 1964). 
5.5.3 
Flammability of Gaseous Mixtures 
5.5.3.1 
Flammable Mixtures 
Mixtures of hydrogen with air, oxygen, or other oxidizers are highly reactive over a wide range of 
compositions. For gaseous mixtures where diffusion is the principal mixing mechanism prior to reaction, 
this range is described by flammability limits, in volume percentage of hydrogen, that define the range over 
which hydrogen vapors will ignite when exposed to an ignition source of sufficient energy. Flammability 
limits are dependent on the ignition energy; temperature; pressure; presence of diluents; size and 
configuration of the equipment, facility, or apparatus; and any other factor that impacts the absorption or 
release of energy within the combustion reaction. 
LH2 or SLH2 as fuel, and liquefied oxygen (LOX) or solid oxygen as oxidizer, do not react on contact, but 
mixtures of these materials have ignited during the mixing process because the energy required to ignite 
them is so small (Bunker, Dees, and Eck, 1995). LH2 and LOX have been detonated by an externally 
generated shock wave. Near stoichiometric combinations that are well mixed can be extremely shock 
sensitive. Comparable experimental examination of SLH2 systems does not exist. 
5.5.3.2 
Flammability Limits 
A flammable mixture may be diluted with either of its constituents, fuel or oxidizer, until the mixture 
concentration falls outside the range within which a flame will continue to propagate after ignition (see 
Figure 6). The mixtures that make up these boundaries are designated flammability limits, with the 
flammable region existing above the LFL or below the UFL.

propagation and narrows for downward flame propagation, a consequence of the high buoyancy of

summary: Comprehensive technical data on hydrogen ignition properties including autoignition temperatures, minimum ignition energy (MIE), flame inhibition, and propagation behaviors in various oxidizing environments. Hydrogen exhibits exceptionally low ignition energy and rapid flame propagation characteristics compared to other fuels, requiring careful safety consideration in system design.

5.5.4 
Ignition of Gaseous Mixtures 
5.5.4.1 
General 
Hydrogen can be easily ignited by a variety of energy sources including flames, hot surfaces, acoustic 
resonances, shock sources, and electric sparks and arcs. An almost imperceptible spark or a static 
electricity discharge may ignite a combustible mixture of hydrogen and an oxidizer (such as air). Two 
important properties related to ignition are (a)  autoignition temperature and (b) minimum ignition energy. 
5.5.4.2 
Autoignition Temperature 
Hydrogen is only slightly more difficult to ignite in air than in oxygen. Ignition temperatures are dependent 
on GH2 concentration and pressure and on the surface treatment of containers. The reported temperature 
is very dependent on the system, and values selected should be applied only to similar systems. At 
101.3 kPa (14.7 psia), the range of reported autoignition temperatures for stoichiometric hydrogen in air is 
773 to 850 K (932 to 1,070 °F); in stoichiometric oxygen, it is 773 to 833 K (932 to 1,039 °F). At pressures 
from 20 to 50 kPa (2.9 to 7.25 psia), GH2 air ignitions have occurred at 620 K (657 °F). 
5.5.4.3 
Minimum Ignition Energy 
Spark discharge energies are used to characterize the ignitability of hydrogen mixtures. The energy 
required for ignition decreases as the mixture of fuel and oxidizer approaches stoichiometry, and increases 
as the mixture pressure decreases below ambient pressure. The MIE is defined as the minimum igition 
energy required for ignition of the most easily ignitable concentration of fuel in air or in oxygen. MIEs for the 
ignition of hydrogen in air and in oxygen at 1 atmosphere are shown in Table 8.

The effects of diluents vary according to the heat capacity and conductivity of the gas species. In air, the 
MIE is increased for species He, CO2, N2, and Ar in the order listed. 
The MIE required for the ignition of hydrogen in air is considerably less than that for methane (0.29 mJ) or 
gasoline (0.24 mJ). However, the ignition energy for all three fuels is sufficiently low that ignition is relatively 
certain in the presence of any weak ignition source, such as sparks, matches, hot surfaces, or open flames. 
Even a weak spark caused by the discharge of static electricity from a human body may be sufficient to 
ignite any of these fuels in air. 
5.5.4.4 
Quenching Gap in Air 
The quenching gap is determined as the greatest physical channel dimension for which flames still cannot 
propagate throughout the channel (Strehlow, 1983) and are cooled to extinction. For hydrogen in NTP, air 
is 0.6 mm (0.024 in.). This dimension depends on the temperature, pressure, and composition of the 
combustible gas mixture and on the electrode configuration. Quenching gap behavior is often the basis for 
the design of flame arrestors. 
Faster burning gases generally have smaller quenching gaps; flame arresters for faster burning gases 
require smaller apertures. The lowest reported quenching distance for hydrogen is 0.076 mm (0.003 in.) 
(Wionsky, 1972). 
There are three major considerations in determining the quenching distance for a gaseous fuel such as 
hydrogen: ignition energy, mixture ratio, and pressure: 
a. Quenching gap is a function of ignition energy. Low ignition energy, 0.001 mJ (9.5 x 10-10 Btu), 
corresponds to a small gap, 0.01 cm (0.0039 in.). Likewise, high ignition energy, 10 mJ (9.5 x 
10-6 Btu), requires a larger gap, 1 cm (0.39 in.) (Van Dolah et al., 1963). 
b. Pressure and composition affect the quenching distance. The quenching distance is closely 
inversely proportional to pressure [d ~ 1/P] (Glassman, 1987). The quenching distance increases 
dramatically at very low pressures. At a distance of several inches, the pressure is barely sufficient 
to support combustion. The effect of mixture ratios is less well known; however, it appears to be 
constant for a given pressure between the UFL and LFL (Van Dolah et al., 1963). Combustion may 
result in pressurization of unburned gases and decrease the quenching distance in a system; 
hence, the placement of flame arrestors is critical (Chelton, 1964). 
c. Specific values for hydrogen-air mixtures are not available; however, the effect of pressure as a 
function of tube diameter for deflagration and detonation of acetylene-air mixtures can be used as 
a guideline (Zabetakis and Burgess, 1961).

5.5.5 
Propagation of Flame in Gaseous Mixtures 
Hydrogen release that leads to the formation of a flammable mixture throughout a region sets the stage for 
a traveling flame. With ignition, the flame proceeds wherever it encounters flammable gas and will leave in 
its wake hot combustion products. In this fashion, the flame is said to propagate. Flame propagation 
behaviors vary according to the nature of confinement that defines the region holding the flammable 
mixture. Noteworthy features of such a region include whether a flame can propagate unobstructed, 
whether it will be intimately confined by walls (or within pipes or ducts), and whether it is subject to partial 
blockage by obstructions such as arrays of pipes and grates. 
With mixtures that form in the open, safety concerns vary with the nature of ignition sources. 
For ignitions that arise from a weak source such as a small electric discharge or flame, fire is the primary 
issue, and concerns include the potential for direct exposure of personnel or infrastructure to high 
temperature reaction products, or IR and UV radiation exposure, if in close proximity to the combustion. 
However, strong ignition sources that induce shock (consider large electric arcs or explosives) in sensitive 
mixtures can give rise to the propagation of deflagration and detonation and present an extreme 
overpressure hazard to personnel and infrastructure.  
Scenarios that create a flammable mixture within a confined volume prior to ignition are of particular 
concern. Rapid flame propagation and high overpressures are highly likely when a sensitive hydrogen and 
oxidizer mixture fills a confined region or volume.  
5.5.5.1 
General 
Combustion within a premixed hydrogen and oxidizer mixture may occur by the interaction of three different 
processes within the flame front: 
 
Laminar burning is the result of flame propagation, but solely by diffusion of radicals into the 
unburned gas, and without significant effects from confining surfaces. 
 
Deflagrations are accelerated flames that proceed at velocities less than the speed of sound 
(subsonic) into unburned gases. Diffusion enhanced by flow arising from the interaction of 
expanding product gases with confining surfaces can, in the right flow geometries, create feedback 
that drives the mixing rate of radicals, increases the burning rate, and accelerates the movement 
of the flame front into unburned gases. When the proper conditions arise, turbulence can lead to 
shock formation, and trigger the detonation process by means of a deflagration to detonation 
transition (DDT). 
 
Shock-driven initiation can give rise to the most energetic combustion process—detonation—which 
is characterized by shock propagation speeds supersonic to the speed of sound in the unburned 
mixture.  
Flame propagation stagnates for mixture compositions that approach the lean and rich limits for 
combustion. The more energetic propagation behaviors require confined sensitive mixtures that approach 
stoichiometry. Examples of confined volumes are pipes and ducts, volumes with dimensions whose 
characteristic length greatly exceeds their width and height. Initiation of combustion within sensitive 
mixtures, even with a low-energy ignition source, can result in a rapid acceleration of the flame. Flame 
propagation can be quenched by passages with narrow dimensions. 
Deflagration and detonation processes have high velocities and can produce high pressures. To the human 
senses, these behaviors appear explosive. Other fuels possess these behaviors, but due to hydrogen's 
rapid molecular motion and ability to mix with other gases, hydrogen exhibits explosive combustion 
behaviors over a wider range of mixtures, is initiated with smaller ignition energies, and possesses flames 
that propagate with greater speed and persist through smaller passages when compared toother fuels. This 
propensity for easily initiated, rapid combustion is a defining characteristic for hydrogen and one that drives 
safety considerations.

title: Section 5.5.5 - Hydrogen Combustion Behavior: Laminar Burning, Deflagration, and Detonation
summary: Comprehensive analysis of hydrogen combustion characteristics including laminar burning velocities, deflagration flame acceleration mechanisms, and detonation limits. Hydrogen exhibits burning velocities 6-7 times faster than hydrocarbons (3.5 m/s stoichiometric in air), with deflagration flame speeds reaching 24-32 m/s in confined geometries and potential detonation velocities of 400-800 m/s. Detonation in hydrogen-air mixtures occurs within 18.3-59% hydrogen concentration range under appropriate confinement and ignition conditions.

42 
5.5.5.2 
Laminar Burning 
The laminar burning velocity is defined as the velocity of unburned gas with given composition, pressure, 
and temperature that flows normal to the flame surface. The measurement of laminar burning velocity is 
performed to obtain a physical constant free of the effects of geometry, fluid flow, and external heat sources 
or sinks (Drell and Belles, 1958). The flame speed, a function of the frame of reference, is a combination 
of the burning velocity and the translational velocity of the bulk flow. Combustion behavior for scenarios in 
which hydrogen, released in the open, forms a flammable mixture, may be compared to the characteristics 
of laminar burning behavior. 
The hazard associated with laminar burning is the propagation of a high-temperature flame throughout the 
region where a flammable mixture persists. Without confinement of the reaction products, high-flame 
velocities do not occur, nor is there overpressure. Burning velocities reported for sensitive hydrogen-air 
mixtures under ambient conditions range between 1 m/s and 3.5 m/s, with peak velocities observed for 
mixtures greater than stoichiometry, approximately 40% v/v (Drell and Belles, 1958, Liu and MacFarlande, 
1961); Figure 10 shows the relationship between hydrogen concentration in air and peak flame velocity. 
The flame velocity increases with temperature (Liu and MacFarlande, 1961) and decreases with pressure 
below atmospheric, but it is nearly constant for pressures between 1 and 4 atmospheres. Experimental 
observations indicate regardless of fuel type that gravity effects may be neglected for laminar burning 
velocities of 20 cm/s and greater (Qiao et al., 2007). 
 
Figure 10 — The effect of hydrogen concentration on burning velocity for hydrogen–air mixtures at 298 K 
(77 F) and 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia)  (Lewis and von Elbe, 1961; Liu and MacFarlane, 1983). 
 
The burning velocity for a stoichiometric hydrogen—NTP air mixture is 3.50 m/s (11.48 ft/s). The high-
burning velocity of hydrogen, approximately six to seven times faster than that of other hydrocarbon fuels 
(NFPA Guide to Gas Safety, 2005), indicates its high explosive potential and the difficulty of confining or 
arresting hydrogen flames and explosions. 
5.5.5.3 
Deflagration 
Deflagration will result in a rapidly moving high-temperature flame and an overpressure. The history of 
pressure and temperature during combustion within a confined volume depends on the total chemical 
energy present and on its rate of release. For flame speeds well below the speed of sound, the rise of

pressure can be assumed to be uniform within a given confinement, with no spatial gradients (Berman, 
1986). Prediction of the effects of deflagration is difficult, due in part to the feedback interaction between 
the confinement and combustion, which in a "real-world" scenario is complex. 
In an isobaric system, the combustion of a stoichiometric mixture of hydrogen-air reactants, initially at NTP 
conditions, will yield an approximate eight-fold volume expansion. Such a volume expansion, if due to a 
centrally positioned ignition, will result in a flame front moving spherically outward relative to a central 
stationary point with a flame speed approximately three times the burning velocity. In a tube sealed at one 
end, a flame speed of nine times the burning velocity, or 24 to 32 m/s (78.7 to 105 ft/s), can occur (Gugan, 
1979). Confinements that feature a “long" dimension (as in a duct or pipe) and that are filled with a sensitive 
mixture (e.g., greater than 12% v/v hydrogen in air) set the conditions for rapid flame acceleration. A 
"bootstrap" mechanism that couples combustion with fluid flow works to cause flame acceleration. In the 
region of ignition, initial expansion of the flame front in the case of weak ignition sources proceeds by a 
diffusion mechanism until the expanding gases encounter confining surfaces. The "near" confining surfaces 
will direct movement of the product gases and the flame into the open direction. This redirection (and 
building flow) works to increase mixing at the flame front and, as a consequence, increases the rate of 
combustion. As flow increases, drag at the wall surfaces impedes movement of the flame near the walls, 
but movement away from the walls is unimpeded. Therefore, the flame front stretches in the free direction, 
and the rate of burning increases further. The expansion can quickly become turbulent, further increasing 
the burning rate. This conceptually simple mechanism—a coupling among combustion, fluid mechanical 
behavior, and confinement—pushes the flame ever faster in the free dimension and is limited only by the 
speed of sound within the gas mixture, or a condition known as choked flow. The flame front can rapidly 
achieve velocities of 400 to 800 m/s. 
Several practical observations are noted about hydrogen-air deflagrations that are derived from energy- 
and geometry-based considerations. The flammable mixture must be sufficiently energetic. The results from 
numerous hydrogen-air combustion tests indicate that high velocities and overpressures do not occur for 
hydrogen concentrations below 12% v/v and greater than 59% v/v (Berman, 1986; Lee, Knystautas, and 
Chan, 1984). For the flame acceleration to occur in tube- or pipe-like geometries, the volume containing 
the flammable mixture must permit the necessary feedback among confining surfaces, expanding 
reactants, and the flame front; specifically, a "length" dimension greater than the cross- sectional area 
(height x width) dimensions must be present to allow the flame front to travel or "run up." Without sufficient 
run-up distance, significant acceleration will not occur. Critical "lengths" are not tabulated as engineering 
data in the literature due to the influence of a number of factors, including not only the gas conditions and 
tubing/pipe sizes, but factors such as wall roughness that are hard to characterize in general. However, 
several relationships based on dimensions in terms of the length/width ratio (L/W), where L is the dimension 
in the direction of flow and W is the characteristic dimension for the cross-section of the volume, have been 
discerned as characterizing acceleration behavior. L/W > 3 may result in some acceleration, L/W > 8 will 
produce acceleration, and L/W > 40 (in smooth-walled confinements) provides sufficient distance to allow 
a run-up or transition to detonation (Woods et.al., 2008). 
Passages with openings or with obstacles separated by regular distances can work to accelerate or retard 
flame accelerations. There are two opposing effects: Formation of turbulence will increase the reaction rate 
and promote acceleration, but a sufficiently large blockage will impede forward propagation of the flame 
front and will increase loss of energy to surrounding surfaces, ultimately preventing propagation of the 
flame. When the barriers occur repetitively, as might be found in an array of pipes within a volume, 
acceleration may be reinforced. The effect of obstacles has been described by a factor known as the 
blocking ratio, the ratio of the obstructed area to the total area of the passage (Lee, Knystautas, and Chan, 
1984).  A variety of behaviors are possible depending on the degree of blockage and acceleration; these 
range from quenching of the flame front, to periodic acceleration and deceleration, to transition, to 
detonation (DDT). 
Several additional caveats apply. Flame propagation requires that the cross-sectional area be greater than 
the minimum required for flame quenching. Increasing turbulence promotes flame acceleration. Surface 
roughness, bends in piping or ducts, and barriers that cause fluid flow to swirl can cause increased

turbulence in fluid flow. Before applying these observed constraints, ignition energy must be considered. 
Powerful shock ignition sources may directly drive flame acceleration and even detonation, and such 
sources will invalidate the relationships that assume ignition sources are weak such that flame acceleration 
occurs incrementally.  
5.5.5.4 
Detonation in Gaseous Mixtures 
5.5.5.4.1 
General 
From the perspective of speed of propagation and overpressure, the worst-case combustion event possible 
is detonation. Given the right conditions, a release of hydrogen (as a gas or cryogenic liquid) into the 
surroundings that contain an oxidizer (usually air), under circumstances that promote formation of a mixture 
capable of supporting detonation, and subject to some form of initiation, detonation can occur. Detonation 
is initiated in one of two ways: directly by shock, which includes sources such as lightning, large electric 
discharges, and explosives, or through a run-up and transition (DDT) of a propagating flame. With the onset 
of the detonation process, the resulting reaction zone is a shock wave, potentially with an accompanying 
blast wave, that presents a very real potential for causing injury to personnel or damage to equipment. 
5.5.5.4.2 
Deflagration-to-Detonation Transition 
Hydrogen–air combustion can start as a detonation, or it can start as a deflagration and then transition to a 
detonation after the flame has traveled for some distance. The composition range in which a detonation 
can take place is narrower than that for deflagration. The commonly quoted range for detonation in a 
hydrogen–air mixture is from 18.3% to 59% hydrogen. However, with higher energy ignition sources, the 
limits can be extended. The factors that influence whether hydrogen-air combustion will occur as a 
detonation rather than as a deflagration include the hydrogen percentage, the strength of the initiator, 
complete or partial confinement of the reaction, and the presence of structures that can induce turbulence 
in the flame front. An energetic source of initiation is required for combustion to start as a detonation. A 
mechanism to accelerate the flame velocity is necessary for a deflagration to transition to detonation. 
Factors that favor this transition include the composition being within the detonation range, a degree of 
confinement, and anything that can induce turbulence in the flame front as it travels through the combustible 
mixture. The latter tends to stretch out the flame front and increase its velocity (Lee et al., 1977). A special 
case of note is when a deflagration combusts into a "dead-headed" volume. This can lead to exceptionally 
high overpressures. Under such circumstances (also described as pressure-piling), the unburned gases in 
the worst case can pressurize to the dynamic pressure produced by the accelerated flame (Nettleton, 1987). 
At such a juncture, should DDT ensue, the worst-case result can be an overpressure that is characterized 
by the multiplicative factors of both deflagration and detonation, beyond the initial pressure within the 
system. 
5.5.5.4.3 
Detonation Limits 
Lower and upper detonation limits vary considerably with the nature and dimensions of the confinement 
and cannot be specified for any fuel and oxidizer mixture unless the nature and dimensions of the 
confinement are also specified (Benz, Bishop, and Pedley, 1988). 
Figure 11 shows the minimum dimensions for detonation of mixtures of hydrogen and air in three types of 
confinement at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia). The figure shows a significant effect of confinement type on 
detonation limits. The ignition energy for detonation also becomes large for lean or rich mixtures; however, 
it is possible to produce overdriven detonations when large ignition energy is introduced. Therefore, 
detonation limits found in the literature should be used with caution. Stable detonations are fairly well 
characterized by the Chapman-Jouguet (C-J) calculation. Annex F, Table F2 gives the type of information 
obtained from such calculations for hydrogen and air mixtures. This table was produced using the Gordon-
McBride computer code (Gordon and McBride, 1994).

Although values of lower and upper detonation limits for GH2-GOX of 15% and 90% hydrogen, respectively, 
are cited (Lewis and von Elbe, 1961), the values suffer from the same shortcomings noted for hydrogen–

5.5.5.4.4 
Detonation Cell Size 
A detonation wave is not a single planar wave front but has a three-dimensional structure consisting of 
cells. The size of the cell, as measured from the two-dimensional pattern left by a detonation on a smoked 
plate, is of considerable value in predicting the onset of detonation and in describing the conditions for 
stable detonation waves. A track from a detonation wave, shown in Figure 12, has passed from left to right, 
producing a “snake skin” appearance from the repeated etching of the cells on the foil. A single cell appears 
as a separately discernible diamond shape.

The cell structure captures the side pattern of a typical multiheaded cellular gaseous hydrogen–air 
detonation. The somewhat irregular cell structure is interpreted as the response of the detonation wave to 
external perturbations, and, that for a given mixture there is only one intrinsic detonation cell width. Cell 
width (b) determination is achieved by examining a large number of cells (Tieszen et al., 1987). 
Dimensions of the cell have been shown to relate to several key parameters in assessing a potential hazard, 
including critical energies and dimensional characteristics of the structural confinement of the detonation 
(Lee et al., 1982). Within the diamond shape of the cell, the length, a, is the dimension in the direction of 
travel and is typically one to two times its width, b, the dimension across the cell vertically. The aspect ratio, 
a/b, increases with decreasing initial pressure. Detonation cell lengths for stoichiometric GH2–air/GOX at 
101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) are 15.9 mm (0.626 in.) and 0.6 mm (0.024 in.), respectively (Bull, Ellsworth, and 
Shiff, 1982). The measurements are specific to the system configuration used.  
Figure 13 gives the variation of detonation cell widths for gaseous hydrogen–air mixtures at 101.3 kPa (14.7 
psia). Ignition energy requirements depend on the concentration of the detonable mixture. Figure 14 gives 
the grams of tetryl required to detonate the gaseous hydrogen–air mixtures shown in Figure 13.

summary: This section provides comprehensive guidance on overpressure prediction from hydrogen combustion events including unconfined combustion, constant volume combustion (AICC), deflagration, detonation, and condensed phase explosions. It establishes overpressure factors for hydrogen-air and hydrogen-oxygen mixtures near stoichiometry and addresses worst-case scenarios including deflagration-to-detonation transition (DDT) with pressure-piling effects.

5.5.6 
Overpressure From GH2 Combustion 
Prediction of specific overpressure consequences of hydrogen combustion events is difficult due to the 
complexity of the factors involved. A simple conservative approach is to evaluate which hydrogen 
combustion processes might play a role in an overall scenario and assess outcomes as the "combined" 
worst-case effects. 
5.5.6.1 
Overpressure in an Unconfined Region 
In general, without initiation sources that produce strong shock waves (such as high explosives or powerful 
electric arcs), flammable hydrogen mixtures ignited in the open—that is, not subject to confinement by 
reflective surfaces—do not produce significant overpressure (Lee et al., 1977). 
5.5.6.2 
Overpressure Due to Combustion Within a Constant Volume (AICC) 
Overpressure due to combustion within a confined volume, but without substantial flame acceleration, can 
be predicted by equilibrium codes programmed for adiabatic isochoric (constant volume) complete 
combustion (AICC) conditions. Maximum values occur near stoichiometry, and "worst-case" overpressures 
for ambient conditions (298 K and 1 atmosphere) may be estimated for hydrogen-air mixtures as being a 
factor of 8 greater than the initial pressure, and a factor of 10.7 (WSTF, 2005) greater than the initial 
pressure for hydrogen–oxygen mixtures. Additional AICC values for the pressure (PAICC) as a function of 
concentration of hydrogen-air mixture and temperature have been tabulated (see Table 1). Overpressures 
of confined hydrogen–air mixtures measured under a variety of experimental conditions generally track 
AICC theoretical values. The experimental results differ from AICC predictions with slightly lower than 
predicted values for lean mixtures (less than approximately 14% v/v hydrogen) and for rich mixtures (greater 
than approximately 42% v/v hydrogen). This difference is thought to indicate incomplete combustion due to 
buoyancy effects. And for sensitive mixtures (approximately 18% to 42% v/v hydrogen) the results show 
slightly higher than predicted values, thought to indicate effects due to the onset of flame acceleration 
(Berman, 1986). AICC code predictions for pressure as a function of hydrogen–oxygen mixture ratios are 
also provided in Table 1. 
5.5.6.3 
Overpressure Arising From Deflagration 
Prediction of specific overpressure consequences of deflagration events is difficult due to the complexity of 
the factors involved. Overpressures can range from none to the C-J detonation pressure (PC-J). Although 
detailed analysis using hydrocodes may produce an accurate assessment of overpressure, a simplified 
approach would be to assume the worst-case outcome and determine C-J values for the mixture of interest, 
or if a range of mixtures is possible, for the mixture that gives the highest pressure. 
Deflagrations propagate within flammable mixtures at subsonic velocities. Bends in lines or pipes, or 
obstacles in the flame path, can act to reflect the pressure wave, causing both superposition of the flame 
front and higher pressure. The final pressure within a confined flame path can range from PAICC to PC-J. 
Unburned gas, trapped by the oncoming flame front of the gas, will pressurize to whatever dynamic 
pressure is achieved by the deflagration, and this may be a value that approaches the C-J pressure. 
Estimates of overpressure that include transition to detonation (DDT) should account for this pressure-piling 
(see Section 5.5.6.5).  
5.5.6.4 
Overpressure Due to High-Pressure Jet Impingement 
Overpressures have been measured in the stagnation regions where an ignited high-pressure release 
impinges on partial confinement such as a solid wall. Guidance on expected overpressures comes from 
limited test research on ignited turbulent jets released from approximately 3,000-psi sources through small 
orifices to impinge upon barriers (Houf et al., 2007; Shirvil and Roberts, 2006). This work suggests 
overpressures in immediate proximity of the confining surface can approach a factor of 2 over the

Head-on impingement of a planar detonation upon a solid surface will cause reflection of the detonation

5.5.7 
Condensed Phase Explosions 
Other phase hydrogen mixtures may support detonation or highly accelerated flames. An example is solid 
oxygen mixed within LH2. Detonations in condensed phases are normally more destructive than gaseous 
detonations because the higher reactant density leads to much greater overpressures (Tarver, 1982). 
Nevertheless, the general properties of condensed phase detonations are very similar to those of gaseous 
detonations (Strehlow, 1968). The detonation may be initiated by a shockwave or by a deflagration, and a 
von Neumann pressure spike followed by a stable C-J detonation wave is observed. Three-dimensional 
cellular structure has been reported for liquids (Dremin, 1969, Tarver 1982); the cellular structure is 
frequently too small to be resolved by present techniques. The analysis of such detonations is difficult 
because the product gases do not obey the ideal gas law at such high pressures and normally differ in 
composition from the products of slow decomposition. In addition, the very high pressures make 
confinement impractical, and they cannot be measured directly (Strehlow, 1968). Tarver (1982) has 
modeled the detonation of a number of condensed explosives using a non-ideal equation of state for the 
product gases and a chemical equilibrium computer code to determine the concentrations of the various 
reaction products in the C-J detonation wave. His highest calculated C-J pressure was 370,000 times 
atmospheric pressure. 
Few common scenarios give rise to such mixtures, and inadvertent creation of such mixtures is to be 
avoided. Collision of launch vehicle storage systems during a failed launch can lead to partial mixing of 
cryogenic fuels. The action of violent mixing initiates ignition so that combustion involves only a small portion 
of the potential reactants in the condensed phase, and the ensuing reaction acts to force the remainder 
apart. The result typically is a fireball involving reaction with surrounding air rather than a condensed phase 
explosion and a limited explosive yield. Containers of liquid oxygen placed within a large pan of liquid 
hydrogen were shattered with explosive detonation cording to simulate the dynamic mixing of hydrogen 
and oxygen possible during a launch accident. The quantity and configuration were varied to simulate the 
potential yield possible from levels of mixing liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen. The results indicate that 
the correlation between the experimental yield and total quantity of propellants mixed is less than predicted 
for theoretical yields (Bunker-Farrah et al., 2003).1 A persistent leak of liquid hydrogen onto the ground can 
chill the ground until condensed air products accumulate. The continued release of LH2 onto the condensed 
air products has been observed to produce an explosive event (Hooker et al., 2011). Another scenario that 
can lead to a mixture of solid air in liquid hydrogen can occur if a Dewar of liquid hydrogen is left directly 
exposed to open air. The rapid volatilization of LH2 to GH2 as it is exposed to ambient temperature air and 
the subsequent mixing of condensed and then solidified air would result in the buildup of solid air in the 
LH2, which at some point would form a detonable mixture. This would persist only until volatilization of 
hydrogen produced mixtures too lean to be detonable. Operations with open Dewars of LH2 are to be 
avoided.  
Solid air mixed in liquid hydrogen is unstable and may detonate, producing effects similar to those of high 
explosives. Mixtures of solid air in liquid hydrogen were found not to detonate for concentrations of less 
than 40%  oxygen (Bowen, 1975). Solid oxygen in excess liquid hydrogen is shock sensitive. A stimulus of 
100 to 250 MPa (19,500 to 36,000 psia) will detonate such mixtures. For comparison, nitroglycerin is 
detonated by 250 to 500 MPa (36,000 to 73,000 psia) shocks (Perlee, Litchfield, and Zabetakis, 1964). No 
rich limits have been reported for LH2-solid air detonations.  
5.5.8 
Energy of Explosion 
The theoretical explosive yield for hydrogen-air is listed below for various forms and units:

a) Approximately 24 g trinitrotoluene (TNT)/g GH2 (24 lb TNT/lb GH2)

title: Hydrogen Hazards - Leaks and Ignition Sources
summary: This section addresses critical hydrogen safety hazards including leak mechanisms, detection challenges, and comprehensive ignition sources. It emphasizes that hydrogen hazards are unique to specific systems and operations, with unwanted combustion events (fire, deflagration, detonation) presenting the greatest consequence threats through high temperatures, overpressure, and blast effects.

c) 0.17 g TNT/kJ GH2 (4 x 10-4 lb TNT/Btu GH2) 
2) NBP LH2–air  
1.71 g TNT/cm3 LH2 (107.3 lb TNT/ft3 LH2) 
It should be emphasized that only a fraction of this theoretical explosive yield will be realized in an actual 
open-air mishap. It is virtually impossible to spill or release a large quantity of hydrogen and to have 
complete uniform mixing with air before ignition. Annex F, Example 3 provides an example of the calculation 
of the detonation characteristics of hydrogen-air-oxygen mixtures using the Gordon-McBride computer 
code (Gordon and McBride, 1994). TNT produces a short-duration, high-impulse pressure wave, whereas 
a hydrogen-air explosion would have a longer-duration and a lower-impulse pressure wave; the external 
effects of the two can be quite different. 
 
Hydrogen Hazards  
This section identifies elements necessary in addressing hazards, but a thorough treatment of how to 
assess hazards and associated risk is beyond the scope of this Guide.  
The hazards associated with hydrogen usage are unique to a particular system and operation. However, to 
promote safety considerations, a brief summary of possibilities is presented. High-pressure hydrogen gas 
and LH2 are man-made fluids, and, from a safety perspective, the hazards that arise during unplanned and 
undesired release are mitigated by intelligent handling, careful operations, and failsafe design. 
Hazards with hydrogen operations are prioritized below: 
1) Unwanted combustion, whether a fire, deflagration, detonation, or combination threaten the 
greatest hazard consequences through exposure of personnel and surroundings to high 
temperatures, overpressure, and blast effects, 
2) Inadvertent release of pressurized hydrogen. Every system that stores hydrogen in gaseous or 
liquid form, is pressurized, and its uncontrolled release is dangerous, 
3) The effects of the low temperatures inherent with liquid hydrogen operations stress components 
through large expansion and contraction in physical dimensions, creation of leak paths when 
sealing surfaces fail, loss of ductility by cold embrittlement and liquid air formation when the 
ambient atmosphere contacts uninsulated cold components, 
4) The effect on metals by hydrogen embrittlement to induce fracture growth and loss of ductility in 
structural elements, such that sudden failure of components can occur and, 
5) When working in proximity to hydrogen, personel are at increased risk of injury due to exposure 
to gas, flame, and cryogenic temperature. 
Safety will be improved when the designers and operations personnel are aware of and take steps to 
mitigate the specific hazards associated with the use of hydrogen. A review of specific issues that have 
arisen in the past is provided.  
5.6.1 
Leaks 
From the perspective of hydrogen infrastructure the fate of stored hydrogen is either to be consumed, or 
released. Releases, whether planned or unplanned (leaks) occur within a system or into the surroundings, 
and by one of two mechanisms. As a pressure difference that drives convection of hydrogen through holes, 
breaks and defects in material surfaces that hold the hydrogen. The openings are many times the molecular 
mean free path, so such convection falls in the continuum flow regime rather than in the molecular flow 
regime. A further differentiation can be discerned between releases driven by low pressure or high pressure 
sources. For hydrogen, if the pressure ratio across the opening exceeds 1.9:1 the through mass flow will

be limited and the exit velocity can't exceed the speed of sound in the gas. Conversely, if the internal 
operating pressure of a system is less than the external pressure, air may leak in. A second mechanism is 
diffusion or permeation, where hydrogen moves through the surface of a confining material, vessel or seals. 
Hydrogen leaks generally originate from valves, flanges, diaphragms, gaskets, and locations where seals 
and fittings are found. Leaks are usually caused by deformed seals or gaskets, valve misalignment, or 
failures of flanges or equipment. The behavior of hydrogen leaks has been characterized (Chernicoff et al., 
2005), and the sizes of hydrogen leaks have been categorized into 5 sizes by industry as according to the 
percentage of opening as compared to the total cross sectional flow area for the line or component in 
question (LaChance et al., 2008). For example, a very small leak is characterized as 0.01% of the total flow 
area, a medium leak 1% of the total flow area, and rupture corresponds to 100% of the total flow area.  The 
likelihood for leaks from lines and components in industrial service has been established by analysis 
(LaChance et al., 2008). 
Leaks usually go undetected because of the absence of a continuous hydrogen monitor in the area. 
Hazardous conditions arise where hydrogen mixes with an oxidizer. Particularly dangerous scenarios 
include: 
 
Slow accumulation of hydrogen in a confined region, 
 
Air or contaminants leaking into a cold hydrogen system (LH2 or SLH2), such as by cryo-
pumping, 
 
A leak may cause further failures of construction materials through cold embrittlement or 
hydrogen embrittlement, and where improper materials have been selected has resulted in 
catastrophic failure. 
For leaks involving LH2, vaporization of cold vapor hydrogen to the atmosphere may provide a warning 
because moisture condenses and forms a fog. 
Undetected hydrogen leaks can lead to fires and explosions. An example of this condition was a large 
sphere partitioned by a neoprene diaphragm with hydrogen stored under the diaphragm and air above it. 
An explosion-proof fan was placed on top of the sphere to provide a slight positive pressure on the 
diaphragm. A violent explosion occurred in the sphere after the plant was shut down. Hydrogen leaked past 
the diaphragm when the fan was turned off. Ignition was attributed to an electrostatic discharge caused by 
motion of the diaphragm or a source associated with the explosion-proof fan. The explosion could have 
been avoided by using an inert gas instead of air across the diaphragm or by monitoring the hydrogen 
concentration in the upper hemisphere. 
5.6.2 
Ignition 
The ignition of GH2–air mixtures usually results in ordinary deflagration. The potential hazards are 
significantly less than if detonation results. It is possible that in a confined or partially confined enclosure a 
deflagration can evolve into a detonation. The geometry and flow conditions (turbulence) have a strong 
effect on the transition from deflagration to detonation. Fires and explosions have occurred in various 
components of hydrogen systems as a result of a variety of ignition sources. Ignition sources have included 
mechanical sparks from rapidly closing valves, electrostatic discharges in ungrounded particulate filters, 
sparks from electrical equipment, welding and cutting operations, catalyst particles, and lightning strikes 
near the vent stack.  Table 11 lists additional ignition sources.
